newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-ALPHAND SHATTERS AUSTRIANS' AURA OF INVINCIBILITY.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-ALPHAND SHATTERS AUSTRIANS' AURA OF INVINCIBILITY.

text.p: Luc Alphand, relaxed after bad weather gave him an unexpected lie-in, became the most successful French downhiller in World Cup history on Friday with his country's first Val Gardena win.

Alphand, who started 17th in a delayed and shortened race, clocked one minute 53.10 seconds for the seventh downhill win of his World Cup career on a cloudy day that shattered the Austrians aura of invincibility.
"Yesterday I saw that France had never won here. I thought it was about time," said Alphand, who had previously shared the French downhill win record with Jean-Claude Killy.

Norwegian Atle Skaardal, in his 11th year on the circuit despite being a year younger than the French downhill World Cup champion, finished second in 1:53.25 while Italy's Kristian Ghedina delighted local fans with third in 1:53.30.
"It's nice to be back among the best downhillers in the world. Its quite a surprise," said Skaardal, whose last podium finish in a World Cup downhill was in 1994.
"I felt before the race that maybe this was my chance. In weather like this anything is possible."

The Austrians, who have dominated the World Cup this season by taking the top four in the opening downhill in Val d'Isere last Sunday and sweeping the leading places in training in France and Italy, were left out in the cold.
Their best finisher was Werner Franz in seventh place, ahead of compatriot Fritz Strobl who won in Val d'Isere.
World and former Olympic champion Patrick Ortlieb of Austria, winner of the last two downhills here, was 17th.
"I'm pleased that the Austrians were behind us today," said Ghedina, who expected them to be back soon.
"They are not like the Italians or the French who have just two or three strong skiers. Its like fighting two against eight or maybe three against 12," the Italian said.
The race was the first of two to be held on the Saslong piste this week, with the second due on Saturday.
It had originally been scheduled for Whistler Mountain in Canada earlier in the month but was postponed because of heavy snow.
On Friday it looked like it would have to be put off again after organisers delayed the start for an hour as clouds shrouded the mountain top and the snow fell steadily.
Many of the skiers and officials had doubted the race would go ahead at all. Alphand was one of them.
"This morning I was pretty sure we would not be racing," he said. "So I stayed in bed in the hotel a bit longer.
Alphand said he had also delayed his arrival at the start because he did not want to be forced to hang around in the noisy, smoky restaurant where others were gathered.
He said the piste had been fine, the visibility less so, and bad weather was something that went with the job.

Alphand's relaxed behaviour at the start was a marked contrast to last year in Val Gardena when he sparked a controversy by being stopped at the start and ordered to change his coloured bib denoting the World Cup downhill leader.
A search revealed that, alone of all the racers, Alphand's spare race bib was missing from the starting hut.
He was eventually allowed to race with his original bib but the incident raised allegations of sabotage, connected to the French nuclear tests in the Pacific at the time.
